short: Direct Bandgap Light Emission from Strained Germanium Nanowi
title: Direct Bandgap Light Emission from Strained Germanium Nanowires Coupled with High-Q Nanophotonic Cavities

lanes.label: Classical tools
lanes.sub: collapsed to one node per state

states.title: Hypothesis and design
states.head: Silicon photonics needs a CMOS-compatible on-chip light source, and germanium is indirect-gap. Whether high tensile strain plus a high-Q cavity can bring Ge to net optical gain is unsettled, with conflicting lasing reports.
states.detail: Absorbed: g1 (HYP/need), g2 (HYP/gap), g3 (HYP/hypothesis), g4 (DES/base_system), g5 (DES/architecture), g6 (DES/variable_sweep), g7 (DES/route), g8 (PRC/forming), g9 (PRC/treatment), g10 (PRC/deposition)

states.title: Structure state
states.head: The fabricated device reproduces the design: an 8 um wire between tapered pads with curved DBR stacks in a 200 nm Ge layer. The wire carries about 2.4% uniform uniaxial tensile strain along its length, from 0.2% in the as-grown layer.

states.title: Property state and mechanisms
states.head: Tensile strain narrows the gap and pulls the direct valley down, while the wire-to-pad strain gradient builds a pseudo-heterostructure that confines carriers in the wire. Direct-gap photoluminescence redshifts from ~1560 nm unstrained to ~1960-1990 nm at 1.95-2.37% strain, more than 400 nm of tuning.
states.detail: Absorbed: g14 (MEC/pathway), g15 (PRP/value), g17 (PRP/value), g18 (MEC/identification). Premises: Tensile strain narrows the Ge bandgap and lowers the direct valley relative to the indirect one; Empirical pseudopotential method used to compute the gain and the individual loss terms

states.title: Performance state
states.head: The cavity delivers resonances with a 24.6 nm free spectral range and a fitted Q of 2020, and the reattached device survives more than ten times the pump power of the free-standing one

states.title: Conclusion
states.head: Strain plus a high-Q cavity gives strong, widely tunable direct-gap Ge emission, but free-carrier and inter-valence-band absorption hold net gain negative, so no lasing is seen

nodes.title: evidence, F4, F5
nodes.head: As pump power rises from 5 to about 48 mW every resonance shifts 10-15 nm to shorter wavelength and broadens, with no linewidth narrowing anywhere. Net gain runs -350 to -1250 cm-1 for the 2.37% device and -520 to -1970 for the 1.95% one between 5 and 22 mW, negative throughout
nodes.solves: Net optical gain stays negative and falls with pump power, though the 2.37% device beats the 1.95% one at every power

panel_conditions.condition: Spectral dependence of the emission on the pump power, each row normalized to its peak
net optical gain versus incident pump power (980 nm CW) for 2.37% and 1.95% strained nanowires

nodes.note: the matching F4c spectra also show a rising background pedestal at 45 mW rather than any threshold behaviour the 1.95% error bars reach about +/-400 cm-1 at 22 mW and the two series nearly touch at 5 mW; the caption puts the 1.95% device at 1961 nm while the text says 1923 nm. The plotted gain is the paper's own reduction of its pump-power measurements, with no OBS parent in this graph, so provenance is measured rather than derived.

nodes.title: evidence, F5
nodes.head: The EPM curve tracks the measured gain-versus-carrier-density points closely above 5e19 cm-3 but runs above them near 2e19. The modelled loss terms cross near 6e18 cm-3: inter-valence-band absorption overtakes conduction-band free-carrier loss and reaches 2.5e3 cm-1 at 2e20, while the pads contribute a flat ~75 cm-1.
nodes.solves: The dominant loss is inter-valence-band absorption, which overtakes conduction-band free-carrier loss above ~6e18 cm-3
nodes.op: compare coplotted quantities, overlay model on data
